questionBank.chapterTitle: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What are the primary functions of the tailwheel in a tailwheel-type airplane?

correct_answers.text: Supports the airplane
Steering
Directional control

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What are the three major handling differences between nose-wheel and tailwheel airplanes?

correct_answers.text: Directional instability
Angle of attack (AOA)
Crosswind weathervaning tendencies

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: How can steering be accomplished in a tailwheel airplane?

correct_answers.text: Airflow on rudder
Propeller slipstream
Mechanical linkage

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: Why are tailwheel aircraft considered inherently unstable on the ground?

correct_answers.text: The center of gravity is located aft of the main gear pivot point
Forward momentum acts to continue and tighten a turn without further steering input
Removing rudder pressure ordinarily does not stop a turn once it has been started

wrong_answers.text: The tailwheel is located forward of the main gear
The center of gravity is located ahead of the main gear
The aircraft lacks a rudder-pedal-operated steering mechanism
Braking action is insufficient to counteract forward momentum
The wide main gear track creates excessive pivot resistance
The tailwheel is fixed and cannot swivel during ground operations
Nose-heavy loading causes the aircraft to veer unpredictably
The propeller torque overwhelms directional control at low speeds

source: AFH Chapter 14, Section 14.2 – Instability

question: What is the purpose of a centering spring or similar device on a tailwheel airplane?

correct_answers.text: It returns the tailwheel to a center position when rudder pedal input is relaxed
It assists pilots in regaining straight-line travel after a turn
It compensates for the tailwheel's tendency to remain deflected after steering input ceases

wrong_answers.text: It locks the tailwheel in a fixed position during takeoff roll
It automatically applies opposite rudder to stop an initiated turn
It prevents the tailwheel from swiveling beyond a set angle
It increases rudder pedal resistance to discourage abrupt steering inputs
It connects the tailwheel directly to the rudder for improved response
It dampens propeller torque effects during ground operations
It ensures the tailwheel remains aligned with the main gear at all times
It replaces differential braking as the primary directional control method

source: AFH Chapter 14, Section 14.2 – Instability

question: What is the correct rudder technique for making a taxi turn in a tailwheel airplane?

correct_answers.text: Apply rudder pressure to initiate the turn
Neutralize the rudder pedals as the turn continues
Apply opposite rudder input to stop the turn and regain straight-line travel

wrong_answers.text: Maintain continuous rudder pressure throughout the entire turn
Use differential braking alone without any rudder input
Apply full opposite rudder immediately after the turn begins
Release all rudder pressure to allow the centering spring to complete the turn
Increase engine power to counteract the tightening tendency during turns
Use nose-wheel steering techniques identical to those used in tricycle-gear aircraft
Apply rudder only after the desired heading is reached to stop the turn
Hold rudder pressure until the aircraft has fully stopped before neutralizing

source: AFH Chapter 14, Section 14.2 – Instability

question: Which statements accurately describe the generation of lift in tailwheel aircraft while on the ground?

correct_answers.text: Tailwheel aircraft generate lift on the ground when there is a relative headwind.
The amount of lift generated by tailwheel aircraft on the ground depends on the wind speed.
Wings and ailerons on tailwheel aircraft aid in liftoff even at slow taxi speeds.

wrong_answers.text: Lift on the ground is exclusive to nose-wheel airplanes.
Tailwheel aircraft only generate lift once airborne.
Ailerons are not involved in ground lift generation.
Ground lift in tailwheel aircraft is independent of wind speed.
This phenomenon simplifies ground handling for tailwheel aircraft.
Only the fuselage contributes to ground lift in tailwheel aircraft.
Ground lift is primarily a concern during high-altitude flight.
Nose-wheel pilots typically anticipate this characteristic.

source: AFH

question: What is the function of a steerable tailwheel in tailwheel-type airplanes during taxiing?

correct_answers.text: Facilitates directional control
Operates along with the rudder
Engages through an arc of about 30° each side of center

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What should a pilot do immediately after beginning to taxi a tailwheel airplane?

correct_answers.text: Test the brakes for proper operation
Apply power to start moving slowly
Retard the throttle and apply brakes smoothly

wrong_answers.text: Use ailerons to lift the wings

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: How should a pilot position the ailerons when taxiing in a quartering headwind?

correct_answers.text: Position ailerons into the wind
Hold the stick into the wind
Kill lift on the upwind wing

wrong_answers.text: Position ailerons away from the wind
Hold the stick away from the wind
Use brakes to stabilize the aircraft

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What is the recommended elevator position when taxiing with a quartering tailwind?

correct_answers.text: Hold the stick away from the crosswind
Position elevator full forward
Reduce upward deflection of elevator

wrong_answers.text: Hold the stick into the crosswind

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What happens to the tailwheel when it is operated beyond its steering arc limit?

correct_answers.text: Breaks free and becomes full swiveling
Allows the airplane to pivot within its own length
No longer provides directional control

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: Why is it important to be aware of wind direction when taxiing a tailwheel airplane?

correct_answers.text: Tailwheel airplanes are vulnerable to surface winds
Wind can lift a wing unexpectedly
Proper control positioning is essential

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What should be done if braking action is unsatisfactory during taxiing?

correct_answers.text: Shut down the engine immediately
Retard the throttle
Apply pressure smoothly to both brakes

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: Which of the following statements are true regarding weathervaning in tailwheel airplanes?

correct_answers.text: Tailwheel airplanes exhibit an exaggerated tendency to weathervane.
Weathervaning describes the tendency of an aircraft to turn into the wind.
The weathervaning tendency is most pronounced when taxiing with a direct crosswind.

wrong_answers.text: Weathervaning is a tendency for an airplane to turn away from the wind.
Nosewheel airplanes are more susceptible to weathervaning than tailwheel airplanes.
The weathervaning tendency is most significant during flight.
Weathervaning makes maintaining directional control easier.
Weathervaning is primarily counteracted by increasing engine power.
The tendency to weathervane is reduced when taxiing with a direct crosswind.
Weathervaning is a phenomenon that only occurs during landing.
Tailwheel steering is always sufficient to counteract weathervaning.

source: AFH Chapter 14

question: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, when taxiing a tailwheel airplane with restricted forward visibility due to its nose-high attitude, what are recommended techniques and initial procedures?

correct_answers.text: Alternately turn the nose from one side to the other (zigzag).
Make a series of short S-turns.
Start all taxi movements with a small turn to ensure no obstructions are directly under the nose.

wrong_answers.text: Maintain a straight taxi path to minimize control inputs.
Increase taxi speed to clear blind spots quickly.
Rely primarily on wingtip clearance for obstacle avoidance.
Keep the aircraft's nose pointed directly at the intended path.
Perform a full 360-degree turn before every taxi segment.
Use only rudder pedals for directional control without turning the nose.
Prioritize maintaining high engine RPM during taxi.
Wait for a ground marshaller to provide continuous guidance.

question: What is a common misconception about maintaining directional control in tailwheel airplanes?

correct_answers.text: Limiting rudder inputs to avoid overcontrolling
Fear of overcontrolling leads to minimal rudder use
Assuming too much rudder use is damaging

wrong_answers.text: Tailwheel aircraft require no rudder input
Directional control is best achieved with ailerons
Rudder inputs should always be minimal
Tailwheel aircraft are damaged by any rudder use
Directional control is maintained by reducing speed
Rudder inputs should be avoided entirely
Tailwheel airplanes do not require pilot input

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14, Section 7

question: During the normal takeoff roll in a tailwheel airplane, which statements correctly describe the procedure for raising the tail?

correct_answers.text: Positive forward elevator should be applied to smoothly lift the tail after a brief period of acceleration
An abrupt pitch change should be avoided because the gyroscopic precession force is directly related to the rate the propeller axis is tilted
The goal of raising the tail is to improve forward visibility and produce a smooth transition to climbing flight

wrong_answers.text: The tail should be raised as quickly as possible to minimize time spent in the three-point attitude
Raising the tail has no effect on directional control because rudder authority is not yet established
The tail should remain on the ground until the airplane reaches rotation speed to prevent gyroscopic effects
Aft elevator should be applied during the initial roll to keep the tail down and improve propeller clearance
Gyroscopic precession from raising the tail produces a right yaw tendency that must be corrected with left rudder
The amount of precession force is unrelated to how quickly the tail is raised
Forward elevator should only be applied after the airplane has reached 70 percent of takeoff speed
Raising the tail reduces forward visibility and should be delayed as long as possible

source: AFH Chapter 14, Section 14.8 – Normal Takeoff Roll

question: Which of the following statements accurately describe directional control requirements during the tailwheel airplane takeoff roll?

correct_answers.text: Directional control should be maintained with smooth, prompt, and positive rudder corrections
Nose-down pitch movement produces left yaw as a result of gyroscopic precession created by the propeller
The increased directional demands of tailwheel airplanes are likely to be unanticipated by pilots transitioning from nosewheel models

wrong_answers.text: Brake pressure should be used as the primary means of directional control during the takeoff roll
Directional control in tailwheel airplanes is easier than in nosewheel airplanes due to the aft center of gravity
Gyroscopic precession during tail raising produces a right yaw that requires left rudder correction
Rudder inputs are unnecessary during the takeoff roll because the tailwheel provides sufficient directional stability
Pilots transitioning from nosewheel airplanes typically find tailwheel directional control easier to manage
Left yaw from gyroscopic precession is corrected by applying left rudder pressure
Brake pressure should be applied smoothly throughout the takeoff roll to assist with directional control
Directional corrections should be made with abrupt, large rudder inputs to stay ahead of yaw tendencies

source: AFH Chapter 14, Section 14.8 – Normal Takeoff Roll

question: Which statements correctly describe throttle and brake management during the normal tailwheel airplane takeoff roll?

correct_answers.text: The throttle should be smoothly and continuously advanced to takeoff power after releasing the brakes
The pilot should carefully avoid applying brake pressure during the takeoff roll
Wing flaps should be lowered prior to takeoff if recommended by the manufacturer

wrong_answers.text: Throttle should be advanced rapidly to full power to minimize the time spent at low speed on the runway
Light brake pressure may be applied throughout the roll to assist with directional control
Flaps should never be used for takeoff in tailwheel airplanes regardless of manufacturer guidance
The throttle should be held at partial power until the tail is raised before advancing to full power
Brakes should be held until full engine power is confirmed before releasing for the takeoff roll
Flap setting for takeoff is determined solely by runway length and is not addressed in the flight manual
Throttle advancement should be paused momentarily when the tail is raised to reduce gyroscopic effects
Brake pressure should be applied intermittently during the roll to maintain runway centerline tracking

source: AFH Chapter 14, Section 14.8 – Normal Takeoff Roll

question: What conditions are necessary for liftoff in a tailwheel airplane during takeoff?

correct_answers.text: Appropriate pitch attitude is maintained
AOA and airspeed combine to produce necessary lift
No additional 'rotation' input is needed

wrong_answers.text: High pitch attitude close to stall

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What should a pilot do during takeoffs in strong, gusty winds?

correct_answers.text: Add an extra margin of speed
Hold the airplane on the ground longer
Make a smooth, positive rotation

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What are essential actions for a crosswind takeoff in a tailwheel airplane?

correct_answers.text: Apply aileron deflection into the wind
Use rudder to prevent weathervaning
Maintain a positive AOA during acceleration

wrong_answers.text: Apply aileron deflection away from the wind
Use rudder to align with the wind
Maintain a negative AOA during acceleration
Keep the wings level throughout the takeoff roll
Rely only on engine power for alignment

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes

question: According to the provided text on short-field takeoffs, which of the following statements are true regarding the technique?

correct_answers.text: Flap settings should be as recommended by the manufacturer.
Initial climb speed should be as recommended by the manufacturer.
After liftoff, the pitch attitude should be adjusted for obstacle clearance.

wrong_answers.text: There are significant differences between short-field and normal takeoff techniques in all aspects.
A three-point attitude liftoff is universally recommended for all short-field takeoffs.
Pilots should prioritize maximum airspeed over obstacle clearance after liftoff.
Manufacturer recommendations for short-field takeoffs are optional guidelines.
The landing gear should be retracted immediately upon rotation.
Short-field takeoffs always require a specific amount of headwind.
The primary goal after liftoff is to maintain a level flight attitude.
Flap settings for short-field takeoffs are always at their maximum permissible setting.

question: What is the purpose of lowering wing flaps before starting a soft-field takeoff?

correct_answers.text: To provide additional lift
To transfer weight from wheels to wings
To minimize drag caused by surface irregularities

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction, Section: Soft-Field Takeoff

question: Why should the airplane be kept in continuous motion on a soft surface during takeoff?

correct_answers.text: To prevent bogging down
To avoid tipping onto its nose
To maintain sufficient power

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction, Section: Soft-Field Takeoff

question: What should be done to maintain a positive angle of attack during a soft-field takeoff?

correct_answers.text: Keep the tail very low
Hold a nose-high attitude
Apply takeoff power smoothly

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction, Section: Soft-Field Takeoff

question: What are key differences in landing between nose-wheel and tailwheel airplanes?

correct_answers.text: Nose-wheel airplanes naturally reduce pitch attitude after touchdown.
Tailwheel airplanes continue to 'fly' in the three-point attitude after touchdown.
Tailwheel airplanes require careful attention to heading, roll, and pitch for an extended period.

wrong_answers.text: Nose-wheel airplanes maintain a constant pitch attitude after touchdown.
Tailwheel airplanes immediately transfer all weight to the tires after touchdown.
Nose-wheel airplanes require more attention to heading and roll after touchdown.
Tailwheel airplanes reduce AOA and remove wing lift immediately after touchdown.
Nose-wheel airplanes continue to 'fly' in the three-point attitude after touchdown.
Tailwheel airplanes naturally reduce pitch attitude after touchdown.
Nose-wheel airplanes require careful attention to heading, roll, and pitch for an extended period.
Tailwheel airplanes are designed so that the wings are beyond critical AOA in the three-point attitude.

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What are important considerations when performing a touchdown in a tailwheel airplane?

correct_answers.text: Ensure the airplane's longitudinal axis is parallel to the runway direction.
Avoid touching down while in a crab or drifting.
Use the three-point or wheel landing techniques appropriately.

wrong_answers.text: Touch down with the airplane's nose pointed slightly off the runway direction.
Allow the airplane to drift during touchdown.
Use only the three-point landing technique.
Touch down with the tailwheel first.
Touch down with the main gear and tailwheel at different times in three-point landings.
Always use a high pitch attitude during touchdown.
Rely solely on the wheel landing technique for all conditions.

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What is the primary goal when performing a three-point landing in a tailwheel aircraft?

correct_answers.text: Attain a steeper fuselage angle
Touch tailwheels and main wheels simultaneously
Maintain flight while slowing

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14

question: What should a pilot do if the main wheels touch down early during a three-point landing attempt?

correct_answers.text: Re-flare the aircraft
Hold the plane off until three-point attitude
Execute a go-around if necessary

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14

question: What is the consequence of holding the aircraft off the ground too long during a three-point landing?

correct_answers.text: Tail makes contact first
Plane pitches forward onto main wheels
Rollout proceeds normally

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14

question: Why is it important to apply full back elevator after the tailwheel makes contact during a three-point landing?

correct_answers.text: Presses the tailwheel on the runway
Prevents lift on horizontal stabilizer
Maintains directional control

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14

question: What are the potential errors when attempting a three-point landing in a tailwheel aircraft?

correct_answers.text: Main wheels touch early
Tail held off too long
Tail touches first

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14

question: What are key characteristics or purposes of a wheel landing?

correct_answers.text: Making contact with the runway at a higher airspeed than a three-point landing.
Landing in a flatter pitch attitude on the main wheels only.
Retaining control authority in some wind conditions.

wrong_answers.text: Landing with the tailwheel touching first.
Requiring a significantly steeper approach angle.
Always involving a full forward elevator input immediately after touchdown.
Having the tail forced down by its own weight for increased lift.
Maintaining a constant back elevator pressure throughout the touchdown.
Being identical to a three-point landing in terms of touchdown timing.
Requiring a lower airspeed than a three-point landing.

question: What are essential elements for a successful wheel landing?

correct_answers.text: A soft touchdown on the main wheels.
A slight relaxation of back elevator just after the main wheels touch.
Permitting the tail to drop on its own accord after main wheel contact.

wrong_answers.text: Forcing the tail down immediately after main wheel contact.
Maintaining a constant pitch attitude until the tailwheel touches.
Pushing forward on the elevator to ensure tail contact.
Initiating a go-around immediately after main wheel touchdown.
Applying full aft elevator before the main wheels touch.
Increasing back elevator pressure immediately after main wheel contact.
Making contact with the runway at a lower airspeed than a three-point landing.
Using a significantly different approach airspeed compared to a three-point landing.

question: What are potential issues or recommended pilot responses related to wheel landings?

correct_answers.text: A high rate of descent can force the tail down, increasing lift.
Pushing forward after a bounce can lead to pilot-induced oscillation.
Initiating a go-around is a recommended response to a bounced wheel landing.

wrong_answers.text: The tail is intentionally forced down by its own weight to increase lift.
The pilot should always push forward to regain contact after a bounce.
A wheel landing always requires a steeper approach angle.
Deceleration should be immediate and aggressive after main wheel contact.
The elevator should be brought to the full aft position before main wheel contact.
There is a significant difference in approach airspeeds between wheel and three-point landings.
The tail should be held off the ground indefinitely after main wheel contact.
Converting to a three-point landing is never an option after a bounced wheel landing.

question: When landing a tailwheel airplane in a crosswind using a sideslip (wing-low) technique, which of the following statements are correct?

correct_answers.text: Only one main wheel makes initial contact at touchdown
Many tailwheel pilots prefer wheel landings in crosswinds because higher touchdown speed makes flight controls more effective
In some aircraft, rudder effectiveness can be reduced by the fuselage and flaps blocking airflow when the tail is low and on the ground

wrong_answers.text: Both main wheels must touch down simultaneously to maintain directional control in a crosswind
A crab angle should be maintained through touchdown to reduce side loads on the landing gear
Three-point landings are generally preferred over wheel landings in crosswind conditions because of better rudder authority
The tailwheel always makes first contact in a crosswind wheel landing
Lower touchdown speed in a wheel landing provides better control authority during crosswind landings
A sideslip approach requires the pilot to align the aircraft with the runway centerline using crab before touchdown
Flaps should always be fully retracted before touchdown in crosswind conditions to improve rudder effectiveness
The wing-low technique requires both main wheels and the tailwheel to contact simultaneously

source: AFH Chapter 14, Section 14.17 – Crosswinds

question: What should a pilot do with the elevator control during the after-landing roll?

correct_answers.text: Hold it back as far as possible
Hold it firmly
Maintain positive control

wrong_answers.text: Use it to lift the nose

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction, Section: After-Landing Roll

question: What can cause a ground loop during the after-landing roll?

correct_answers.text: Loss of directional control
Drift or crab
Aggravated, uncontrolled turn

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction, Section: After-Landing Roll

question: How should a pilot apply brakes during the after-landing roll?

correct_answers.text: Slide toes up from rudder pedals
Apply heel pressure if equipped
Avoid releasing rudder pressure

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction, Section: After-Landing Roll

question: What should be done if a wing starts to rise during the after-landing roll?

correct_answers.text: Apply aileron control toward the rising wing
Lower the rising wing
Adjust ailerons based on speed

wrong_answers.text: Apply aileron control away from the rising wing

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction, Section: After-Landing Roll

question: When should the pilot retract the flaps after landing?

correct_answers.text: After the airplane is stopped
When clear of the landing area
After turning onto a taxiway

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction, Section: After-Landing Roll

question: During a crosswind after-landing roll in a tailwheel airplane, what actions are crucial for maintaining directional control and preventing the upwind wing from rising?

correct_answers.text: Using rudder for directional control.
Using tailwheel steering for directional control.
Applying aileron to keep the upwind wing from rising.

wrong_answers.text: Decreasing aileron input as the airplane decelerates.
Allowing the upwind wing to rise slightly to relieve stress.
Holding aileron control neutral throughout the roll.
Increasing engine power to improve rudder effectiveness.
Relying solely on differential braking for directional control.
Applying elevator control to maintain nose attitude.
Reducing rudder input as the airplane slows down.
Ignoring the crosswind component once on the ground.

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: Which statements accurately describe the characteristics and pilot actions during a crosswind after-landing roll in tailwheel airplanes?

correct_answers.text: The airplane tends to weathervane into the wind.
Weathervaning tendency is more prevalent in tailwheel-type airplanes.
Aileron control should be held fully toward the wind when the airplane is coming to a stop.

wrong_answers.text: The airplane tends to turn away from the wind during the roll.
Ailerons become more effective as the airplane decelerates.
Less aileron input is required as the airplane slows down.
The airplane's profile area is greater forward of the main landing gear.
The crosswind component becomes less critical during deceleration.
The main wheels act as a pivot point for the airplane's nose.
The upwind wing experiences a decreasing lifting force from the crosswind.
Pilots should operate in wind conditions exceeding the airplane's capability.

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What are the key actions to perform during a short-field landing in a tailwheel airplane?

correct_answers.text: Hold the airplane in a three-point attitude upon touchdown
Apply brakes evenly and firmly after touchdown
Close the throttle immediately upon touchdown

wrong_answers.text: Maintain a nose-high attitude upon touchdown
Apply brakes only after reaching taxi speed
Keep the throttle partially open after touchdown
Use only aerodynamic braking without applying brakes
Touch down with one wheel first
Rely solely on reverse thrust for stopping
Ignore the use of brakes to minimize roll
Apply brakes unevenly to steer the airplane

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes

question: During a soft-field landing in a tailwheel airplane, which of the following statements are correct?

correct_answers.text: The tailwheel should touch down simultaneously with or just before the main wheels
Firm back-elevator pressure should be maintained throughout the landing roll to prevent nosing over
The pilot may need to increase power after touchdown to prevent the airplane from becoming stuck in the soft surface

wrong_answers.text: The main wheels should touch down well before the tailwheel to improve directional control
Brakes should be applied firmly immediately after touchdown to minimize rollout distance
The tailwheel should be held off the surface as long as possible after the main wheels touch down

The throttle should be reduced to idle before touchdown to avoid propeller strike risk on soft terrain
Power should be reduced immediately after touchdown to prevent the airplane from becoming airborne again
A wheel landing technique is preferred over a three-point landing on soft fields

source: AFH Chapter 14, Section: Soft-Field Landing

question: What factors can initiate a ground loop during ground operations in a tailwheel airplane?

correct_answers.text: Side-load on landing
Taxi turn with excessive groundspeed
Uneven ground surface

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

question: What corrective actions should a pilot take to prevent a ground loop from developing?

correct_answers.text: Firm rudder input
Differential braking
Prompt removal of corrections

source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes Introduction

correct_answers.text: Ground operations
Takeoffs
Landings
